anchor: O Mother Race! to thee I
title: Publication and address
short: Published in Dunbar's first book, Oak and Ivy (Dayton, 1893), and reprinted in Lyrics of Lowly Life (1896); an ode to the African American people.
body: Dunbar, then about twenty and working as an elevator operator in Dayton, paid for the printing of Oak and Ivy himself. The ode addresses the race as a mother, 'Ethiopia', and offers a 'pledge of faith'. It was written a generation after emancipation, in the years when Reconstruction's gains were being reversed. Historians of Black nationalist thought have called it a kind of anthem of the period's racial pride.

sources.cite: Paul Laurence Dunbar, Oak and Ivy (Dayton, Ohio, 1893), full text, African American Poetry: A Digital Anthology (Lehigh University)
Paul Laurence Dunbar, Lyrics of Lowly Life, with an introduction by W. D. Howells (New York: Dodd, Mead, 1896); text as in The Complete Poems of Paul Laurence Dunbar (1913), Project Gutenberg
Joanne M. Braxton, ed., The Collected Poetry of Paul Laurence Dunbar (University Press of Virginia, 1993), introduction and notes
Wikipedia, 'Ode to Ethiopia' (publication and summary)

title: Ethiopia
short: In biblical and nineteenth-century usage 'Ethiopia' stood for Africa and its peoples generally; Psalm 68:31 made it a sign of providential hope.
body: In the King James Bible 'Ethiopia' translates Hebrew Kush, the lands south of Egypt, and Greek Aithiopes ('burnt-faced') named dark-skinned peoples in general. Psalm 68:31, 'Ethiopia shall soon stretch out her hands unto God', became a key text for nineteenth-century African American and African thinkers, a tradition historians call Ethiopianism, which read it as a prophecy of the race's rise. Dunbar's title and the closing 'Ethiopia's glory' place the poem in that tradition, though the poem itself does not quote the psalm.

sources.cite: The Bible, Authorized (King James) Version, Psalm 68:31
Wilson Jeremiah Moses, The Golden Age of Black Nationalism, 1850-1925 (Hamden, CT: Archon Books, 1978), on Ethiopianism

title: Stanza form
short: Six-line tail-rhyme stanzas (aabccb): two tetrameter couplets each followed by a shorter line with feminine rhyme.
body: The pattern, with the short third and sixth lines rhyming on two syllables ('glory/gory', 'growing/blowing'), is a form of the tail-rhyme stanza used in medieval romance and in hymns. Its regularity suits a public ode intended for recitation. The feminine endings give each stanza a lift at its close. Internal rhymes appear too ('On every hand in this fair land', 'To right they cling; the hymns they sing').

sources.cite: Joanne M. Braxton, ed., The Collected Poetry of Paul Laurence Dunbar (University Press of Virginia, 1993), introduction and notes
Peter Revell, Paul Laurence Dunbar (Twayne, 1979)

anchor: When Slavery crushed thee with its
title: Slavery's heel
short: Slavery as a tyrant trampling the race; the image may recall the serpent whose head is bruised by the heel in Genesis 3:15.
body: Being crushed under a conqueror's heel is a common image of oppression. Some readers hear an inversion of Genesis 3:15, where the woman's seed will bruise the serpent's head while it bruises his heel, so that the race's suffering anticipates its eventual triumph; this is a possible echo rather than a certain allusion. The first stanza ends on 'gory', establishing the motif of blood that returns in the 'severe baptism' of stanza 6.

sources.cite: The Bible, Authorized (King James) Version, Genesis 3:15
Joanne M. Braxton, ed., The Collected Poetry of Paul Laurence Dunbar (University Press of Virginia, 1993), introduction and notes

title: The plant of freedom
short: Freedom is imagined as a plant that grew secretly from seed during slavery and is now in blossom.
body: The organic metaphor implies that emancipation was prepared by long, hidden growth, an optimistic reading of history. 'Blowing' (l. 12) means blooming, an older sense of the verb. The image fits the title of the book, Oak and Ivy, and the confident tone of the post-war generation, though readers have noted how its springtime optimism contrasts with the violence of the early 1890s.

sources.cite: Oxford English Dictionary, s.v. 'blow, v.2 (to bloom)'
Joanne M. Braxton, ed., The Collected Poetry of Paul Laurence Dunbar (University Press of Virginia, 1993), introduction and notes
Peter Revell, Paul Laurence Dunbar (Twayne, 1979)

title: Ethiope
short: A poetic form of 'Ethiopian'; the race's children stand beside their 'fairer' (lighter-skinned) neighbours.
body: 'Ethiope' is the older English form used in poetry and in Jeremiah 13:23 ('Can the Ethiopian change his skin...?'). 'Swarthy' simply means dark-complexioned. The stanza pictures Black Americans standing 'beside' whites, with a pun on 'fairer' as both paler and, implicitly, not more just. Their labour in forests, smithies and fields claims a share in the building of the nation.

sources.cite: The Bible, Authorized (King James) Version, Jeremiah 13:23
Oxford English Dictionary, s.v. 'Ethiop, n. and adj.'
Joanne M. Braxton, ed., The Collected Poetry of Paul Laurence Dunbar (University Press of Virginia, 1993), introduction and notes

title: Honest labour
short: The race's progress is pictured in work: clearing forests, forging, farming.
body: The stanza reflects a post-emancipation ideology of uplift through industry, later associated especially with Booker T. Washington, whose Atlanta address came two years after the poem. 'Labour' and 'honour' are spelled in the British way in this text. Some critics find the vision accommodating, emphasising work and patience over protest; others see it as a claim to citizenship earned by contribution.

sources.cite: Joanne M. Braxton, ed., The Collected Poetry of Paul Laurence Dunbar (University Press of Virginia, 1993), introduction and notes
Peter Revell, Paul Laurence Dunbar (Twayne, 1979)
Booker T. Washington, Up from Slavery (1901), ch. 14, 'The Atlanta Exposition Address'

anchor: Their voices sound through senate halls
title: Senate halls
short: Probably recalls Black legislators of Reconstruction, such as Hiram Revels and Blanche K. Bruce of Mississippi, the first Black U.S. senators.
body: During Reconstruction African Americans were elected to state legislatures and to Congress; Hiram Revels entered the U.S. Senate in 1870 and Blanche K. Bruce served a full term from 1875 to 1881. By 1893, when the poem was published, Black political representation in the South was being destroyed by disfranchisement, so the line's present tense is partly commemorative and partly hopeful.

sources.cite: United States Senate, Historical Office, 'Hiram Revels' and 'Blanche Kelso Bruce'
Joanne M. Braxton, ed., The Collected Poetry of Paul Laurence Dunbar (University Press of Virginia, 1993), introduction and notes

anchor: Thy name is writ on Glory's
title: Glory's scroll
short: The race's name is written in fire on the roll of fame, an image of lasting honour.
body: The 'scroll' of glory recalls the biblical book of life in which names are written (Revelation 20:12) and the classical roll of fame. 'Characters of fire' are letters of flame, an image suggesting both visibility and divine writing (compare the writing on the wall in Daniel 5). The 'banner' in the next lines turns the stanza into a military triumph.

sources.cite: The Bible, Authorized (King James) Version, Revelation 20:12; Daniel 5:5
Joanne M. Braxton, ed., The Collected Poetry of Paul Laurence Dunbar (University Press of Virginia, 1993), introduction and notes

title: Baptism of blood
short: Suffering in slavery, and perhaps Black soldiers' blood in the Civil War, is a baptism that purifies the race's 'spotless robes'.
body: The robes 'washed... white in the blood of the Lamb' belong to the martyrs in Revelation 7:14, and Christ speaks of his coming death as a baptism (Mark 10:38). Dunbar applies this martyr imagery to the race collectively, which makes its suffering redemptive. Many readers also connect 'blood' with the nearly 200,000 Black soldiers and sailors who served the Union.

sources.cite: The Bible, Authorized (King James) Version, Revelation 7:14; Mark 10:38
Joanne M. Braxton, ed., The Collected Poetry of Paul Laurence Dunbar (University Press of Virginia, 1993), introduction and notes
Peter Revell, Paul Laurence Dunbar (Twayne, 1979)

title: chrism
short: Consecrated oil used in anointing; the sweat of forced labour becomes a holy anointing.
body: From Greek chrisma, 'anointing', related to Christos, 'the anointed one'. Chrism is used in baptism, confirmation and ordination in the older churches. The conceit turns the sweat of enslaved labour into a sacrament and makes the race Christ-like, bearing a cross on its brow (l. 34). Some readers see in the cross the figure of Simon of Cyrene, the African who carried Christ's cross (Mark 15:21), though the poem does not name him.

sources.cite: Oxford English Dictionary, s.v. 'chrism, n.'
The Bible, Authorized (King James) Version, Mark 15:21
Joanne M. Braxton, ed., The Collected Poetry of Paul Laurence Dunbar (University Press of Virginia, 1993), introduction and notes

title: Forgiveness
short: The claim that no other race so seldom grieved or so readily forgave has been read both as moral triumph and as conciliatory reassurance to white readers.
body: Dunbar praises the race for not 'stooping to grieving' under torture ('the rack') and for forgiving once free. Some critics argue that this flatters a white audience that wished to hear that the formerly enslaved bore no resentment, a theme of the post-war 'plantation' imagination. Others read the stanza as asserting moral superiority: the forgiving race 'proved them men', a claim to full humanity. 'Or white or black' means 'whether white or black'.

sources.cite: Joanne M. Braxton, ed., The Collected Poetry of Paul Laurence Dunbar (University Press of Virginia, 1993), introduction and notes
Peter Revell, Paul Laurence Dunbar (Twayne, 1979)
Henry Louis Gates Jr., Figures in Black: Words, Signs, and the 'Racial' Self (Oxford University Press, 1987), on Dunbar and dialect

anchor: From bards who from thy root
title: Bards from the root
short: The poet foresees future poets of the race telling its story; 'root' recalls the messianic 'rod out of the stem of Jesse'.
body: Isaiah 11:1 prophesies that 'there shall come forth a rod out of the stem of Jesse, and a Branch shall grow out of his roots'. Dunbar adapts the image to a line of poets springing from the race. The stanza is self-referential: the young poet presents himself as one such bard, and later readers have seen the Harlem Renaissance as fulfilling the hope. 'List' means listen to.

sources.cite: The Bible, Authorized (King James) Version, Isaiah 11:1
Joanne M. Braxton, ed., The Collected Poetry of Paul Laurence Dunbar (University Press of Virginia, 1993), introduction and notes
Peter Revell, Paul Laurence Dunbar (Twayne, 1979)
